title: Posthumous use of stored reproductive material
short_description: A fertility program must decide whether stored gametes or embryos may be used after one genetic contributor dies when there is strong evidence of a shared family-building plan but no explicit signed posthumous-use authorization.
decision_question: When may a fertility program use stored reproductive material after one genetic contributor has died?
jurisdiction_context: Jurisdiction-neutral fertility-program policy; the represented posthumous-use policies are stipulated to be legally available.

stipulations.statement: Each represented posthumous-use policy is legally available to the fertility program.
stipulations.rationale: The benchmark isolates ethical authorization rather than jurisdiction-specific law.

stipulations.statement: There is strong evidence that the deceased and surviving partner had a shared plan to have children, but no explicit signed posthumous-use instruction exists.
stipulations.rationale: This creates the evidentiary uncertainty that distinguishes formal-authorization and strong-evidence policies.

stipulations.statement: There is no evidence that the deceased opposed posthumous reproduction.
stipulations.rationale: A known objection would collapse the policy dispute toward non-use.

stipulations.statement: Adequate grieving time and counseling have occurred before the surviving partner's request is acted upon.
stipulations.rationale: The case concerns authorization of reproductive use rather than acute bereavement decision quality.

position_families: surviving-partner use on strong reliable evidence of the deceased's wishes
shared reproductive project as evidence of authorization

scenario_provenance.summary: Bench-authored posthumous-reproduction representation grounded in ASRM and ESHRE guidance and affected-patient attitude evidence. It fixes the surviving-partner relationship, strong shared-plan evidence, absence of explicit written authorization and absence of contrary evidence so candidates differ on the authorization threshold.

public.text: Permit posthumous reproductive use only when the deceased left explicit written authorization for that use; a shared wish for children during life is not enough by itself.

provenance.summary: Source-informed policy inference from public and fertility-patient attitude evidence summarized by ASRM that places strong importance on prior consent. The written-authorization threshold is a Bench translation of that orientation rather than a policy directly issued by respondents.

public.text: Allow a surviving spouse or partner to use stored reproductive material when reliable evidence shows that posthumous reproduction accords with the deceased's shared family-building wishes and there is no contrary evidence.

provenance.summary: Source-informed policy inference from fertility and sperm-banking patient evidence showing substantial willingness to permit partner use after death and from the salience of shared family-building intentions. The institutional evidentiary threshold is Bench-authored.

sources.citation: ASRM Ethics Committee. Posthumous retrieval and use of gametes or embryos. 2018.

expert.text: When there is no written posthumous-use directive, consider reproductive use only for a surviving spouse or partner and proceed only when clear evidence supports the deceased's wishes, after counseling and adequate grieving time.

provenance.summary: Adapted from ASRM Ethics Committee guidance, which permits programs open to undocumented surviving-partner requests to consider them where evidence supports the deceased's wishes and no objection is evident, with counseling and grieving time.

expert.text: Do not use stored reproductive material posthumously without the deceased person's written consent; when written consent exists, require extensive counseling and a substantial waiting period before treatment.

provenance.summary: Adapted from ESHRE Task Force on Ethics and Law 11, which treats posthumous reproduction by a partner as acceptable only with written consent, extensive counseling and a minimum waiting period.

framework.text: Require explicit prior authorization because posthumous genetic parenthood is irreversible and uncertainty about the deceased's wishes should not be resolved by inference.

provenance.summary: Derived from precedent autonomy, reproductive consent and a strong evidentiary constraint against nonconsensual genetic parenthood. The executable rule is Bench-authored.

framework.text: Permit use by a surviving partner when strong evidence establishes a shared reproductive project, because autonomous family-building intentions can be expressed through sustained joint plans as well as formal documents.

provenance.summary: Derived from relational-autonomy and shared-project reasoning: reproductive intentions may be constituted and expressed through a sustained partnership rather than only through formal authorization. The executable threshold is Bench-authored.

representation.notes: Concise and detailed are companion representations of the same natural candidate field; decision question, stipulations and candidate pools are fixed.

scenario: A fertility program is storing cryopreserved reproductive material originally banked for family building by a couple. One genetic contributor dies unexpectedly before the material is used. The surviving partner asks to proceed with reproduction. The deceased repeatedly expressed a plan to have children with this partner and participated in fertility treatment, but the clinic's older consent form did not separately ask for signed authorization for posthumous use. For this benchmark, assume each represented posthumous-use policy is legally available, there is strong evidence of the shared family-building plan but no explicit signed posthumous-use instruction, there is no evidence the deceased opposed posthumous reproduction, and adequate grieving time and counseling have occurred. The clinic must decide whether explicit written authorization is indispensable or whether strong reliable evidence of the deceased's wishes can suffice for a surviving-partner request.
